observation.visible_scene: A wide, very calm lake or bay under an overcast sky. In the foreground a white metal railing runs along the left (a dock/pier edge) and a small piece of white railing appears at the right edge. A dense clump of reeds grows out of the water at left-of-center with a thin diagonal pole/stick leaning through it; additional reed clumps sit at the far left and far right edges. Across the water a low, tree-covered shoreline dotted with a few houses (one with a blue roof) forms the horizon. A single small dark waterbird (duck/coot-like) floats on the open water in the right-center of the frame.
visible_changes: The floating bird drifts slowly and steadily toward the left (toward the center of the frame) relative to the fixed background shoreline and the right-edge reeds; its vertical position on the water surface stays essentially unchanged.
A faint horizontal wake/trail is visible to the right of the bird in several frames, consistent with the bird moving leftward across the still water.

The water surface shows only minor, slowly evolving ripples; the reflection of the central reed clump and pole in the water shifts and distorts slightly frame to frame, but no object is added or removed.

The camera is static: the foreground railing, the diagonal pole tip, the left/right reed clumps, and the distant houses hold the same pixel positions from the first to the last frame, so the bird's leftward shift is object motion, not camera pan.
outside_clip_unknowns: Whether the bird is actively swimming/paddling or merely being carried by a gentle current or wind is not determinable from the frames.
The bird's intended direction or destination beyond the right edge of the cropped segment is unknown.
Events before t=0 and after the last frame (e.g., whether the bird stops, dives, or exits the view) are outside the excerpt.
uncertain_details: A tiny dark speck appears high in the sky in a few mid-clip frames (around the upper-right area); it may be a distant flying bird or a sensor artifact, but its nature and motion are not reliably established.
The exact speed of the bird's drift is small (tens of pixels over ~2.6 s) and hard to quantify precisely.
Subtle changes in the water's reflected pattern are present but cannot be separated cleanly from compression noise.

may already be underway in the first view and may continue beyond the last. The endpoints need
NOT match or connect as a loop. Do not judge different endpoints as a physical inconsistency,
and do not invent a trigger, contact, start, stop, landing, disappearance or completion to make
the excerpt form a complete story. Missing context outside this segment stays unknown.
If an editing cut is visible inside the segment, distinguish it from continuous physical motion;
do not invent a smooth transition or a causal mechanism to connect the two views.
Describe what is visible during the excerpt, the actual changes, and supported persistent
properties. Cover the main visible process, not just scenery. Distinguish object movement from
camera movement, reflection from separate objects, expansion from translation, deformation from
occlusion, and an already ongoing process from its onset. Only state what the clip supports;
do not invent causes, an earlier impact, an unseen operator, material identities or later outcomes.
Do not infer motion from one frame, a visible seam or a single pose. Static intervals are valid.
Do not supply named physics laws. Compare each important entity's first and last image positions
and their relative positions before describing motion. Treat camera motion as uncertain when the
background evidence is insufficient, and retain clear relative changes despite that uncertainty.

"outside_clip_unknowns":["unseen prerequisites or outcomes, only when relevant"],
"uncertain_details":["..."]}. Be concrete and concise, in English. This is not a complete event reconstruction.
